title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6981 – Reuters estimate
body: The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run. --- Earlier: Goldman Sachs says yuan undervalued by up to 25% and markets underestimate how far it can rise --- The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.Summary: The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets.

title: Standard Chartered custody for Ripple's RLUSD: what custody and collateral mirroring mean for traders
body: Standard Chartered will now hold Ripple's dollar-pegged stablecoin, RLUSD, for institutional clients through its branch in the Dubai International Financial Centre. The bank also plans to let those clients use RLUSD as trading collateral at LMAX Group without the tokens ever leaving the bank. That second part is not live yet. Together, though, the two pieces show how traditional finance is trying to fix one of crypto's oldest problems: what happens to your money when the venue holding it fails. To see why this matters, it helps to unpack three ideas: stablecoins, custody and collateral. What happened The bank announced on Monday that it now supports institutional custody of RLUSD issued on the XRP Ledger. The service runs through its DIFC branch, which is regulated by the Dubai Financial Services Authority. Separately, Standard Chartered has joined a planned integration with LMAX Group, a London-based marketplace for currencies and crypto, that would make RLUSD eligible collateral on agreed LMAX products. What is RLUSD? A stablecoin is a crypto token designed to hold a steady value, in this case $1. RLUSD is backed by US dollars, US government bonds and cash equivalents. Ripple launched it in December 2024 on both Ethereum and the XRP Ledger, a public blockchain closely associated with Ripple. The bank's new service covers only the XRP Ledger version. RLUSD has grown to a market value of roughly $2.45 billion.

title: Germany September final CPI +3.3% vs +3.3% y/y prelim
body: German September final CPI +3.3% vs +3.3% y/y prelim Prior +2.9% Germany September final HICP +3.3% vs +3.3% y/y prelim Prior +2.9% The headline readings are unrevised compared to the preliminary estimates, but they do reaffirm that German headline inflation has climbed back above the 3% threshold at the end of the third quarter. Energy inflation is the main culprit, rising 3.8% within the month and is 14.9% more expensive compared to the same month last year. This marked the third consecutive month of year-on-year increases in energy prices (August 2026: +10.5%; July 2026: +8.3%; June 2026: +3.4%) and the highest since February 2023. Core annual inflation is seen at 2.4%, keeping steady relative to August at least. So, that at least provides some comfort that the surge in energy prices isn't broadening all too much - yet. Services inflation continues to be a key sticking point, seen at 2.7% in September, even if it has cooled from above 3% earlier in the year. But even at this rate, it is still underpinning core inflation in keeping that above the 2% threshold. For now, the ECB can take comfort in that core prices aren't surging again in Europe's largest economy. But as higher energy prices continue to feed through, the risk of spillover effects will continue to rise. And that means the risks of second-round effects to the inflation outlook will also gather pace, the longer that this trend keeps up. This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

title: Why a few bad trades can undo weeks of trading profits
body: You can have a good trading strategy and even get most of your trades right. But as we've seen, that doesn't necessarily mean that you'll be profitable at the end of the day. If you're constantly taking profits too early and worse still, letting your losses run wild, that's a recipe for disaster when it comes to trading. We've all been there, myself included, in letting losses consume you and give you a false sense of hope in believing that things might turn around. It's a slippery slope. Some of us are perhaps lucky enough to walk away with just a painful lesson. But for others, this is the thing that takes you out of the game entirely. It all comes down to trading discipline at the end of the day. Let's go back to the apple store example again (I told you, I love my apples). Imagine that you buy apples from a supplier at $10 each and hope to sell them for $15 each. That's a potential profit of $5 per apple. Now, business is moving along well and customers are buying apples daily. But after a few days, you get nervous that your customers might just disappear. And instead of waiting to sell at $15 the next day, you quickly sell them for $12. You still happily pocket the $2 profit, so that doesn't sound too bad right? I mean, at least you're making money. But now, let's picture the other side of the scenario. Let's say business suddenly turns sour and nobody wants your apples, so the market price drops to $7 each.

title: BoE's Greene warns waiting for second-round inflation effects would be too late
body: Greene's remarks reinforce the hawkish wing of the MPC and support market expectations of a November hike, which recent reports put at around 84%. Her warning about second-round effects ties directly to the energy shock from the Iran war: if higher oil and diesel costs feed into wages and pricing, the case for tightening strengthens further, keeping short-dated gilt yields and sterling sensitive to energy prices. The comments also add pressure on the gilt market at a time when global bond yields are already elevated. Upcoming UK wage and inflation data will be key for whether her view gains wider support on the committee. -- Greene's message is simple: by the time inflation shows up in wages and prices, it will be too late, so the Bank should move before it gets there.

title: Goldman sees Europe reserve release cutting diesel by $11 but shrugs off Russian supply
body: Diesel remains the sharpest pressure point in the energy shock from the Iran war, and Goldman's view suggests relief depends on government stockpiles rather than extra Russian barrels. A European reserve release of the scale Goldman models would offer meaningful but temporary relief, narrowing refining margins and easing pressure on transport and industrial costs feeding into inflation. The bank's broader view that product markets stay tight into 2027 means any relief rally in diesel could prove short-lived, keeping crack spreads elevated and refiners' margins strong. For crude, a sustained diesel squeeze keeps demand for refinery runs high, supporting oil prices even if headline supply fears ease. --- Earlier: More on Russia's diesel U-turn: 500,000 tons cleared for export after Trump-Putin deal IEA urges faster diesel releases as 400m-barrel March pledge lags, board meets Oct 15 ---- Goldman's message on diesel is that Europe's emergency stockpiles can take some heat out of prices, but Moscow's offer won't, and the underlying shortage is not going away soon.

title: Australian business confidence slides to -13 as oil shock and rate hikes bite, NAB says
body: Oil is the main pressure point: volatility tied to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and the broader Iran conflict is lifting costs and denting sentiment, so any further energy spike would likely push confidence lower still. The survey highlights the RBA's dilemma, with businesses souring under higher funding costs even as the central bank, according to minutes released today, worries about domestic capacity pressures and rising business inflation expectations. Weak confidence could argue for caution on further hikes, but the RBA has signalled it is prepared to tighten again if inflation stays sticky, leaving the Australian dollar and short-dated yields sensitive to upcoming inflation data. Mining's relative resilience suggests resource-linked equities may continue to outperform domestically focused sectors. title: AI compute crunch deepens as chip rental costs jump 60% and rivals scramble for power
body: The squeeze hands pricing power to anyone who already controls chips, data centres and electricity, favouring hyperscalers, neoclouds and chipmakers over the startups trying to rent from them. Rising rental prices and tougher contract terms point to stronger near-term revenue for compute providers, but also to growing concentration risk, as only the biggest and best-funded labs can lock in capacity. The rush to overbook capacity as a hedge raises the danger of a sharp reversal if demand disappoints, leaving firms stuck with costly lease commitments and a glut of resold capacity. That fragility echoes recent warnings that financing, power and data centre delays, not demand, are now the binding constraints on the AI build-out. --- Earlier: Broadcom CEO likens AI boom to a casino even as he targets $230 billion in chip sales Goldman Sachs flags power and compute as two chokepoints in the AI boom --- AI's real shortage is not ideas or money but raw computing power, and the scramble for it is turning rivals into partners, executives into deal brokers and startups into casualties.

body: BlackRock's shift adds weight to the case that higher yields are starting to compete with equities for capital, a dynamic that could cap stock valuations even as earnings stay strong. Conversely, a further oil spike that lifts this week's CPI and PPI could push yields higher still and test the cushion BlackRock estimates before Treasury returns turn negative. title: RBA minutes show three reasons for hike to 4.60% and leave door open to further increases
body: The minutes read hawkish, not unexpectedly, with the board explicitly keeping further hikes on the table and markets already pricing roughly another 15 basis points by year-end and 30 basis points in the first half of 2027. Oil is central to the outlook: domestic fuel prices were running well above the RBA's August assumptions, and any further escalation of the Iran war would feed directly into the risk of more tightening. The board's concern that a lagging RBA could weaken the Australian dollar suggests it is willing to keep pace with other central banks, which should support the currency against a backdrop of rising global yields. Rate-sensitive sectors such as banks, property and consumer discretionary remain vulnerable, given falling house prices and the board's view that household spending must stay subdued for some time. --- The RBA has concluded the economy is running hotter and the neutral rate is higher than it thought, which is central bank language for "we may not be done yet".

title: Japan wholesale inflation misses at 6.8% but stays high enough to keep BOJ hike alive
body: The miss trims some urgency from the hike narrative, but an annual pace near 7% and surging import costs leave the case for tightening intact, keeping Japanese yields and BOJ pricing sensitive to any hawkish signals. The weak yen is the key amplifier: with oil prices elevated by the Iran war, every leg lower in the currency raises the yen cost of energy and feeds back into pipeline inflation. A rate hike that narrows the gap with other central banks could support the yen and ease that pressure, which is part of the case for acting sooner. Traders will watch whether firms keep passing higher costs through to consumer prices, the step the BOJ watches most closely. --- Japan's factory-gate inflation came in softer than feared, but with the weak yen pushing import costs up by a quarter, the pressure behind a BOJ hike has not gone away.

title: Bitcoin sellers had a go but could not push the lower targets
body: Bitcoin moved lower yesterday, breaking below its 100-hour moving average and approaching the bottom of the swing area at $81,183. The low reached $81,388, falling short of that key downside target before buyers stepped back in. Sellers had their shot. They missed. The rebound subsequently carried the price above the 100-hour moving average at $82,997 and the 200-hour moving average at $83,545. However, buyers could not sustain the upside momentum. The price has since slipped back between those two technical levels. Moving averages become the barometers With bitcoin sandwiched between the hourly moving averages, traders have clear levels to define risk and judge who is taking control: Above the 200-hour MA at $83,545: The bias becomes more bullish. Buyers would then look toward resistance near $84,236, corresponding with Monday's high and today's high area. Getting above—and staying above—that level would give the rebound more credibility. Below the 100-hour MA at $82,997: The bias shifts back toward the sellers. The downside focus returns to yesterday's low at $81,388 and the swing-area floor at $81,183. Below that, the September 19 low at $80,106 becomes the next key target. For beginner traders, the distinction is between crossing a moving average and holding beyond it. Today's rebound crossed both averages, but the failure to stay above the 200-hour MA shows that buyers still have work to do.

title: Is the AI bubble bursting?
body: Nostradamus has been dead for centuries, but his followers are still around, especially in finance, with Ray Dalio warning that the AI bubble may be close to bursting as interest rates rise and tech companies take on massive debt to build AI infrastructure. Are we heading for another dot-com crash? Things do seem to be getting murkier for the sector, with OpenAI's annualized revenue reaching around $50 billion at the end of September, $20 billion below the previously expected $70 billion. As concerns grow that AI demand may be slowing and revenues may not justify massive infrastructure investments, Oracle, Microsoft, and Nvidia shares, alongside the Nasdaq-100, have naturally come under pressure. This week, selling pressure also spread to semiconductor and tech stocks across Asian markets. Chinese chipmaker CXMT's progress in developing a new memory architecture has raised concerns about growing competition for global memory makers. On top of that, Broadcom's CEO compared AI investors to casino gamblers, suggesting some don't fully understand what they're betting on, and warned that financing AI infrastructure could become a major challenge. Looking ahead, high Treasury yields could add fuel to the fire by making riskier AI stocks less attractive to investors. Still, this isn't a classic bubble, as massive infrastructure spending is backed by real growth in revenue, orders, and contract backlogs.

title: Long global semiconductors remains the most crowded trade followed by short US Treasuries, according to Bank of America
body: The latest Bank of America Global Fund Manager Survey showed investors have become less optimistic about the macroeconomic outlook, while positioning in technology stocks remains near its most extreme level in six years. The survey was conducted between October 2 and October 8 among 161 participants managing $453 billion in assets. The Bank of America Global Fund Manager Survey (FMS) is one of the most influential monthly reports in the financial world. It polls roughly 200 to 400 institutional fund managers (people managing hundreds of billions of dollars in hedge funds, pension funds, and mutual funds) to see how they are positioned in the markets. The survey is often used as a contrarian indicator because extreme positioning can reveal where consensus trades are vulnerable to disappointment. However, crowded positioning alone is not a sufficient reason to bet against a trend. The opportunities come when stretched positioning coincides with a catalyst that changes market expectations. Fund managers are now more overweight technology stocks than at any point since August 2020. The proportion of respondents overweight the sector increased to 37% from 30% in September, while global semiconductors remain the most crowded trade. At the same time, investors have made their largest reduction in bank exposure since March 2023. Although sentiment has weakened, investors are still broadly positive on the macroeconomic outlook.

title: Connecting the dots: How the AI boom could turn into the Fed's next inflation headache
body: Here's some food for thought. What if I told you that amid all the excitement about AI and how it is transforming our lives, some of that could eventually show up on your electricity bill? That would be interesting, no? Let's break it down and take a look at how that might turn out to be the case in reality. Now, when we talk about AI, we tend to imagine smarter chatbots, robot innovation, and tech stocks taking off to the moon. However, there's a much less glamorous side to all of that. I mean, somebody has to be the one to build enormous buildings to house all those computers, and then also keep them running around the clock. Yes, I'm talking about data centres here. And these buildings need electricity to work and cooling systems to stop them from overheating. So, picture this. You have tens of these buildings now suddenly turning up in the same town; that is in fact what is happening across the globe. Now, the local power grid wasn't necessarily built for that much demand in mind. As such, the utility company might have to bring in more power, upgrade substations and lay new cables. Those things are not cheap. And depending on how some of those costs are shared, some of the bill could end up with households and businesses. And it's not just electricity, either. These projects need plenty of raw material like steel and copper, alongside specialised equipment and skilled construction workers.

body: The euro appears to be catching a bit of a break against the franc this week, though I'm not entirely convinced that the danger has passed just yet. But as we get into the new week, the pair managed to bounce off the key technical region around 0.9300 with the 100-day moving average (red line) and trendline support from the March and May lows helping to provide an additional layer of defense for buyers. So, the question now is whether buyers can build on that rebound or if this is merely a temporary reprieve. A firm break below that would put the 200-day moving average (blue line) around 0.9236 in focus next, before potentially opening up a move towards the 0.9200 level. The key risk for the currency pair? It is the fact that the French-German bond yield spread continues to stay elevated around 141 bps, not far from the recent highs near 150 bps. The wider yield spread suggests that investors are still demanding a hefty premium to hold French debt, with fiscal concerns continuing to outweigh confidence. And the longer that this situation persists, the greater the risk that some of the unease we're seeing could spill over into other euro area bond markets. For now, we're certainly not quite at the stage to label this as another euro area debt crisis.

title: Fed's Collins says uncertainty is elevated as she watches breadth of inflation pressures

title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - China inflation data
body: China releases consumer and producer price data for September at 0130 GMT on Wednesday, which is 9:30 pm US Eastern time on Tuesday. Factory-gate inflation is the reading most likely to move markets, as higher global energy costs continue to feed through the economy. August sets the benchmark. Consumer prices rose 0.8% y/y, up from 0.5% and in line with forecasts, while the 0.4% monthly gain beat expectations. Producer prices climbed 3.8% y/y from 3.5%, with the statistics bureau pointing to rising energy prices. There are three things to watch. The first is producer prices. The August increase reflected imported inflation, with higher crude oil and non-ferrous metal prices lifting petrochemical and smelting prices at home. Another firm print would confirm that the oil shock is still working its way through Chinese input costs. The second is pass-through to consumers. Headline CPI remains well short of Beijing's informal target of around 3%. Analysts warn that a weak property sector and soft consumption make it hard for downstream manufacturers to pass on higher costs, and that factory prices could slip back towards deflation once supply-side support fades. A widening gap between strong PPI and modest CPI would point to a squeeze on margins, not demand-led inflation. The third is core CPI, which excludes food and energy. It gives the clearest read on whether domestic demand is firming or whether energy is doing all the work.

title: US CPI: Energy prices expected to lift headline inflation. Will core stay contained?
body: The US CPI report for September will be released tomorrow at 8:30 AM ET. The report - along with the PPI on Thursday - will give traders another key piece of the inflation puzzle as markets assess whether the Fed will need to tighten policy further. Number crunchers will also be able to get a handle on the PCE and Core PCE from both readings. The expectations are seeing: Headline CPI month over month: +0.6% expected versus +0.4% last month. Headline CPI year over year: +3.6% expected versus +3.4% last month. Core CPI month over month: +0.2% expected versus +0.3% last month. Core CPI year over year: +2.5% expected versus +2.4% last month. The core numbers will be the focus. A 0.1% MoM (or better) core and 2.4% (or better) YoY would be moving in the right direction.. The key question: How far are energy costs spreading? Higher energy prices are expected to drive the stronger headline reading. The more important question for the broader inflation outlook is whether those costs are filtering into other goods and services. That puts the core reading—which excludes food and energy—firmly in focus. Last month, gasoline prices rose 3.9%, accounting for more than one-third of the monthly headline increase. However, core prices also rose 0.3%, with increases in categories including airline fares, lodging and used vehicles. Traders will be watching whether those underlying pressures ease in September.

The key word is "currently." The inflation data still need to support his outlook. If price pressures remain stubborn, that policy assessment can change. title: USDCHF ping-pong's between support and resistance targets
body: The USDCHF has been playing ping-pong between support and resistance over the last six trading days, confined to a range between 0.8290 and 0.8348. That is just 58 pips, with neither buyers nor sellers able to sustain a break. Yesterday, both extremes were tested. Support held near 0.8291, while resistance near 0.8348 capped the rally into the close. Today, sellers leaned against that topside resistance in the Asia-Pacific session and pushed the price toward two interim support targets: The 100-hour moving average at 0.8322. The 200-hour moving average at 0.83156. The low reached 0.8313, briefly dipping below both moving averages before quickly bouncing higher. Sellers had their shot below the moving averages, but could not sustain the break. That puts the moving averages in focus as the close barometer for buyers and sellers. Stay above both, and buyers have room to push back toward the 0.8348 ceiling. Move below both and stay below, and sellers would take more control, opening the door for another test of support near 0.8290. For now, the broader range remains intact. The moving averages help traders judge which side has the advantage within that range, but a sustained break of the floor or ceiling is needed to move beyond the ping-pong trading. title: Goldman sees upside risks (105 EUR!) to its 70 euro TTF gas forecast as Europe stocks run low
body: Europe's gas market is now tied directly to the same Gulf disruption that is driving crude, so escalation in the Middle East lifts both energy risk premia together. If Europe has to outbid other regions for LNG this winter, the strain falls hardest on price-sensitive importers in Asia and emerging markets, tightening the global market further. Higher gas prices also feed through to European power costs and industrial margins, adding to inflation pressure. The upside skew also strengthens the economic case for burning oil products instead of gas where switching is possible, a modest extra support for diesel and fuel oil demand. --- Goldman's base case still sees European gas easing to 70 euros, but low storage and shrinking Mideast LNG flows mean the risks point the other way. Summary: Goldman Sachs says risks to its year-end TTF forecast of 70 euros per megawatt hour are skewed to the upside Low European inventories and a month-on-month drop in Middle East LNG exports have supported TTF in the mid-80s In a low-supply scenario with average weather, the bank estimates winter TTF would need to peak near 105 euros/MWh to cut enough LNG demand outside Europe Goldman says uncertainty over winter weather widens the range of possible price outcomes further Goldman Sachs sees the risks to its year-end forecast for European natural gas prices tilted to the upside, as low storage levels and falling Middle East LNG exports leave the region exposed heading into winter.

title: Morgan Stanley lifts Brent forecast to $105 as costly freight favours short-haul crude
body: The freight argument points to Brent holding a firmer premium over long-haul grades, including WTI delivered into Europe, for as long as shipping stays expensive. Refiners in Northwest Europe benefit from cheaper delivered barrels from Brazil, West Africa and the US, while producers of those grades absorb the cost through weaker differentials. The main risk to the call is a sustained fall in freight rates, for example from a durable normalisation of Hormuz traffic, which would remove the Brent-specific support even if overall supply stays tight. Traders should watch tanker rates and physical differentials as closely as the flat price. --- Earlier: Catch up time!
